tagline: Turquoise water beside a shore road from Garden City to Laketown
intro: Bear Lake Scenic Byway follows US 89 from the Idaho line to Garden City, then SR-30 beside the lake toward Laketown. Utah’s tourism office presents the shore drive as a chance to see turquoise water and sandy beaches, with raspberry milkshakes in Garden City during summer. It lists the SR-30 trip between the two towns as ten miles and fifteen minutes. The lake straddles Utah and Idaho, and its turquoise-blue color comes from suspended calcium carbonate deposits.

The road east of Garden City entered the state highway system in 1910, on the stretch to Sage Creek Junction. The state designated the Laketown Scenic Byway in April 1990. Its northern reach changed in June 2002, when Logan Canyon received National Scenic Byway status. The US 89 section between Garden City and Idaho was transferred from Logan Canyon’s state designation to the extended, renamed Bear Lake Scenic Byway.

Traveling south from the state line brings you to Garden City, where SR-30 branches from US 89. The road follows Bear Lake’s south shore to Laketown. The lake’s southern end was a gathering place for fur traders and Native Americans in 1827 and 1828. The designated drive ends at East Shore Road in Laketown.

moments.title: Bear Lake
moments.text: Bear Lake’s turquoise-blue color comes from suspended calcium carbonate, the mineral in limestone. The lake occupies a depression formed by fault movement, a process that continues to deepen its eastern side. It is at least 250,000 years old. Human engineering has also changed its water: in 1911 a diversion redirected most of the Bear River’s flow into the lake through Mud Lake. The connection allows its upper 21 feet to store spring runoff for irrigation later in the year. Before that engineered connection, the lake had been separated from the Bear River for 11,000 years.

moments.title: Garden City
moments.text: Horatio Nelson Jackson and Sewall Crocker stopped in Garden City in 1903 on the first automobile journey across the United States. The lakeshore town had been settled in 1877; in 1979 it merged with neighboring Pickelville. Expansion of the water system prompted that merger. Garden City also celebrates the valley’s raspberry harvest with its annual Raspberry Days festival. Raspberry Days generally falls in the first week of August and includes parades, a craft fair and a raspberry recipe cookoff. Utah’s tourism office singles out the town’s raspberry milkshakes as a summer stop along SR-30.

moments.title: Laketown
moments.text: The south end of Bear Lake, in the area of present-day Laketown, hosted the Rocky Mountain Rendezvous in 1827 and 1828. Trappers, trade-goods suppliers and Native Americans from several tribes gathered to exchange furs for supplies. Jedediah Smith arrived in June 1827 after an overland round trip to California. His journal records that his party had been given up as lost. Rendezvous Beach takes its name from those summer trading gatherings. The beach forms part of Utah’s Bear Lake State Park, whose other recreation areas include Bear Lake Marina and East Side.
